questions.stem: A web server is overwhelmed by a flood of TCP SYN packets. Every packet in the capture comes from the same IP address, 203.0.113.50. Considering only the number of sources, which term describes this attack?

options.text: DoS
options.rationale: Correct: a single source makes it a DoS, whatever technique it uses.

options.text: DDoS
options.rationale: A DDoS comes from many distributed sources; this capture shows one.

options.text: Botnet
options.rationale: A botnet is a group of compromised devices; only one address is involved here.

options.text: Coordinated attack
options.rationale: A coordinated attack involves multiple actors acting together.

questions.explanation: The SYN technique is a distractor. Counting sources decides the label: one source is a DoS, and only many distributed sources would make it a DDoS.
questions.discriminator_tested: DoS has one source; DDoS has many distributed sources.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes how a botnet is typically used to carry out a DDoS?

options.text: Devices are compromised; they join the botnet and check in with a C2 server; the C2 server issues an attack command; the devices flood the target
options.rationale: Correct: recruit, take orders through C2, then attack.

options.text: The target is flooded; devices are then compromised; the C2 server is set up afterward
options.rationale: The flood is the result, so it cannot come before the devices are recruited.

options.text: The C2 server floods the target directly; afterward the botnet recruits more devices
options.rationale: The C2 server sends orders; the flood comes from the botnet's many devices.

options.text: Devices flood the target on their own; then the attacker compromises them to stop the flood
options.rationale: Bots act on the attacker's commands; they are compromised before they attack.

questions.explanation: A botnet is the means: compromised devices that take orders through a command and control channel. The DDoS is what the attacker then makes the botnet do.
questions.discriminator_tested: The botnet is the army (the means); C2 gives the orders; the DDoS is the attack.

questions.stem: Analysts confirm that infected hosts are receiving orders from an external command and control server. While the hosts are being cleaned, which action most directly cuts off the attacker's control?

options.text: Block outbound traffic to the C2 server's domains and IP addresses at the firewall
options.rationale: Correct: without the control channel, the hosts cannot receive new orders.

options.text: Change the native VLAN on trunk links
options.rationale: That counters double-tagging VLAN hopping, not malware check-ins.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping on the switches
options.rationale: That stops rogue DHCP servers, not traffic to an attacker's server.

options.text: Block common passwords
options.rationale: That counters dictionary attacks; the hosts are already compromised.

questions.explanation: Command and control (C2) is the channel the attacker uses to send orders. Blocking it isolates the compromised hosts from the attacker while they are remediated.
questions.discriminator_tested: C2 is the control path; cutting it removes the attacker's control.

questions.stem: A network monitor reports a sudden traffic spike on the company's main website. Which two statements about this alert are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: On its own, it shows a symptom and cannot identify the cause
options.rationale: Correct: a spike is an observation, not a diagnosis.

options.text: It could be caused by legitimate demand, such as a product launch
options.rationale: Correct: legitimate surges also produce spikes.

options.text: It always indicates a DDoS attack
options.rationale: A spike can be malicious or legitimate, so 'always' is wrong.

options.text: It proves the web server has joined a botnet
options.rationale: Nothing about incoming volume shows that the server itself is compromised.

options.text: It means the server's firmware has been corrupted
options.rationale: Corrupted firmware describes a permanent DoS, which a volume alert cannot show.

questions.explanation: A traffic spike is only a symptom. Its cause may be an attack or legitimate demand, so it must be investigated before it is classified.
questions.discriminator_tested: A traffic spike is a symptom; the cause may be malicious or legitimate.

questions.stem: Which statement about a coordinated attack is NOT accurate?

options.text: All of its traffic must come from a single source
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is inaccurate: a coordinated attack involves multiple sources or actors.

options.text: It involves multiple sources or actors acting together
options.rationale: Accurate: this is the definition.

options.text: It overlaps with the idea of a DDoS
options.rationale: Accurate: both involve many sources.

options.text: Its defining emphasis is synchronization between the sources
options.rationale: Accurate: timing together is the focus of the term.

questions.explanation: A coordinated attack is multiple sources or actors acting together. It overlaps with DDoS, but the term stresses synchronization; a single source would be neither.
questions.discriminator_tested: Coordinated attack = multiple actors, emphasis on synchronization.

questions.stem: An internal file server becomes unresponsive every night at 01:00. Investigators find that a misconfigured backup job on every workstation starts at the same minute and saturates the server. No attacker is involved. What is the best classification?

options.text: Friendly (unintentional) DoS
options.rationale: Correct: a misconfiguration exhausted the resource, with no malicious intent.

options.text: Coordinated attack
options.rationale: The jobs are synchronized, but there is no attacker or intent.

options.text: Botnet
options.rationale: The workstations are not under an attacker's control.

options.text: Permanent DoS
options.rationale: The server recovers each night once the backups finish; nothing is permanently damaged.

questions.explanation: A friendly or unintentional DoS is an outage with no malicious intent, such as viral demand, a misconfiguration, or a runaway process. Intent is the differentiator.
questions.discriminator_tested: Friendly DoS: no attacker; intent is the differentiator.

questions.stem: Which control most directly reduces the risk of someone cutting cables or switching off equipment in a wiring closet to take the network down?

options.text: Locked, access-controlled wiring closets with camera monitoring
options.rationale: Correct: a physical threat needs a physical control.

options.text: New IPS signatures
options.rationale: An IPS inspects traffic; cutting a cable produces no attack traffic to inspect.

options.text: DHCP snooping
options.rationale: DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP servers, not hands on equipment.

options.text: Regular OS patching
options.rationale: Patching fixes software flaws; it cannot stop someone cutting a cable.

questions.explanation: A physical attack hits availability by damaging or powering off infrastructure and generates no network traffic, so network tools cannot stop it. Physical access controls can.
questions.discriminator_tested: Physical attacks hit availability with no network traffic, so they need physical controls.

questions.stem: In outage 1, a router stops responding during a traffic flood and recovers as soon as the flood stops. In outage 2, a router stays unusable after the attack until it is reflashed. Which pair of labels is correct?

options.text: Outage 1: DoS; outage 2: permanent DoS
options.rationale: Correct: only outage 2 needed a reflash to recover.

options.text: Outage 1: permanent DoS; outage 2: DoS
options.rationale: This is reversed; outage 1 recovered without repair.

options.text: Both are permanent DoS
options.rationale: Outage 1 recovered when traffic stopped, so it was not permanent.

options.text: Outage 1: physical attack; outage 2: rootkit
options.rationale: Outage 1 was a traffic flood, and a rootkit wants a working device to hide in.

questions.explanation: A permanent DoS corrupts firmware so the device needs a reflash or replacement. A reboot or the end of the traffic does not fix it, unlike an ordinary flood.
questions.discriminator_tested: A PDoS needs a reflash or replacement; an ordinary DoS ends when the flood stops.

questions.stem: Which configuration change stops a network from being used as the amplifier in a Smurf attack?

options.text: Configure routers not to forward ICMP echo requests sent to directed broadcast addresses
options.rationale: Correct: without broadcast echo requests, the many hosts never reply to the victim.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping on access switches
options.rationale: That stops rogue DHCP servers, not ICMP broadcasts.

options.text: Increase the server's half-open TCP connection table
options.rationale: That relates to SYN floods, which use TCP, not ICMP.

options.text: Change the native VLAN on trunk links
options.rationale: That counters double-tagging VLAN hopping.

questions.explanation: A Smurf attack sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source, so every host replies to the victim. Refusing to forward broadcast echo requests removes the amplifier.
questions.discriminator_tested: Smurf depends on ICMP echo requests reaching a broadcast address.

questions.stem: Which two observations point to a SYN flood rather than a Smurf attack? (Choose two.)

options.text: TCP SYN packets arrive, but the three-way handshake is never completed
options.rationale: Correct: this is the SYN flood technique.

options.text: The server's half-open connection table is full
options.rationale: Correct: unfinished handshakes fill this table.

options.text: ICMP echo replies from many hosts flood the victim
options.rationale: That is the Smurf pattern.

options.text: Echo requests are being sent to a broadcast address
options.rationale: That is how a Smurf attack recruits replies.

options.text: The victim's IP appears as the spoofed source of ICMP requests
options.rationale: That is also a Smurf indicator.

questions.explanation: A SYN flood abuses the TCP handshake and fills the half-open connection table. A Smurf attack uses ICMP echo to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed source.
questions.discriminator_tested: SYN flood fills the half-open TCP table; Smurf uses ICMP broadcast replies.

questions.stem: An attacker spoofs the victim's IP address and sends requests to thousands of third-party servers running a simple echo service. Each server sends the victim a response about the same size as the request. Which term fits best?

options.text: Reflective attack
options.rationale: Correct: third parties bounce the traffic, but there is no size gain.

options.text: Amplified attack
options.rationale: Amplification needs responses larger than the requests; these are the same size.

options.text: Smurf attack
options.rationale: Smurf specifically uses ICMP echo to a broadcast address.

options.text: SYN flood
options.rationale: A SYN flood abuses the TCP handshake on the target server itself.

questions.explanation: Reflective attacks bounce spoofed requests off third-party servers toward the victim. They become amplified only when each response is larger than its request.
questions.discriminator_tested: Reflective = a third party bounces it; amplified = the response is larger than the request.

questions.stem: A traveler often works on public Wi-Fi. Which measure most directly stops an on-path attacker on that network from reading or altering the traveler's web sessions?

options.text: Using encrypted, authenticated connections such as HTTPS
options.rationale: Correct: the attacker may still sit in the path but cannot read or undetectably change the traffic.

options.text: Choosing a longer account password
options.rationale: A long password sent over an unencrypted session can still be read.

options.text: Upgrading the laptop's firmware
options.rationale: Firmware fixes device flaws; it does not protect traffic crossing the network.

options.text: Blocking common passwords
options.rationale: That counters dictionary attacks, not interception.

questions.explanation: An on-path attacker sits between two parties to read or alter a live session. Encryption with authentication protects confidentiality and integrity even when the attacker is in the path.
questions.discriminator_tested: On-path attacks break confidentiality and integrity of a live session; encryption counters them.

questions.stem: Which statement about DNS poisoning is NOT true?

options.text: It only works if malware is installed on the user's computer
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: the false record sits in a resolver or cache, not necessarily on the user's PC.

options.text: A user can type the correct domain name and still reach the wrong IP address
options.rationale: True: this is the hallmark of DNS poisoning.

options.text: False records are inserted into a resolver or its cache
options.rationale: True: this is how the attack works.

options.text: Poisoning a shared resolver can misdirect many users at once
options.rationale: True: everyone using that resolver gets the false answer.

questions.explanation: DNS poisoning inserts false records into a resolver or cache, so users who type the right name reach the wrong IP. No malware on the user's machine is required.
questions.discriminator_tested: DNS poisoning: right name typed, wrong IP reached, via a poisoned resolver or cache.

questions.stem: A switch port connected to a user's PC suddenly forms a trunk link with the switch, and the PC begins receiving traffic from several VLANs it is not assigned to. Which attack is this?

options.text: VLAN hopping by switch spoofing
options.rationale: Correct: the PC pretends to be a switch and negotiates a trunk.

options.text: VLAN hopping by double tagging
options.rationale: Double tagging sends frames with two tags and abuses the native VLAN; no trunk is formed.

options.text: ARP spoofing
options.rationale: ARP spoofing redirects traffic within one subnet; it does not reach other VLANs.

options.text: Rogue AP
options.rationale: A rogue AP is an unauthorized wireless access point, not a trunk negotiation.

questions.explanation: VLAN hopping reaches VLANs you are not assigned to. Switch spoofing does it by negotiating a trunk; double tagging does it by exploiting the native VLAN.
questions.discriminator_tested: Switch spoofing forms a trunk; double tagging exploits the native VLAN.

questions.stem: On a LAN, the ARP caches of several PCs show the default gateway's IP address mapped to the MAC address of an unknown workstation, and their internet traffic now passes through that workstation. What is happening?

options.text: ARP spoofing
options.rationale: Correct: forged ARP replies map the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC.

options.text: DNS poisoning
options.rationale: DNS poisoning corrupts name-to-IP records; here the IP-to-MAC mapping is wrong.

options.text: Rogue DHCP
options.rationale: A rogue DHCP server would hand out a different gateway IP; here the gateway IP is correct.

options.text: VLAN hopping
options.rationale: VLAN hopping reaches other VLANs; this traffic stays on the local subnet.

questions.explanation: ARP spoofing sends forged ARP replies so the attacker's MAC is linked to another host's IP, here the gateway. It works only on the local subnet and commonly sets up an on-path attack.
questions.discriminator_tested: ARP spoofing corrupts IP-to-MAC mappings on the local subnet.

questions.stem: Users are reaching the internet through an attacker's machine instead of the real router. Which finding shows that a rogue DHCP server, not ARP spoofing, is the cause?

options.text: The users' IP settings list an unexpected default gateway address that was assigned when they got their lease
options.rationale: Correct: the wrong gateway was handed out in the DHCP configuration.

options.text: The users' settings list the correct gateway IP, but their ARP caches map it to an unknown MAC
options.rationale: That is ARP spoofing: the configuration is right, but the MAC mapping is forged.

options.text: Users typing correct domain names reach the wrong IP addresses
options.rationale: That points to DNS poisoning.

options.text: The users' PCs show 169.254.x.x addresses
options.rationale: That means no DHCP server answered at all.

questions.explanation: A rogue DHCP server hands out bad gateway or DNS settings at lease time. ARP spoofing leaves the settings correct and forges the IP-to-MAC mapping instead.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rogue DHCP changes the assigned settings; ARP spoofing forges the MAC mapping.

questions.stem: Which two actions most directly reduce the IoT vulnerabilities that let attackers recruit smart devices into botnets? (Choose two.)

options.text: Change default credentials before the devices are deployed
options.rationale: Correct: default logins are a leading way IoT devices are taken over.

options.text: Keep the devices' firmware up to date
options.rationale: Correct: unpatched firmware is the other common IoT weakness.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping on the switches
options.rationale: That stops rogue DHCP servers, not device takeovers.

options.text: Change the native VLAN on trunk links
options.rationale: That counters double-tagging VLAN hopping.

options.text: Install an ad blocker on office PCs
options.rationale: That may reduce malvertising on PCs but does nothing for the IoT devices.

questions.explanation: Default credentials, unpatched firmware, and weak or missing encryption are the typical IoT vulnerabilities. Fixing the first two removes the easiest routes into a botnet.
questions.discriminator_tested: IoT devices are recruited through default credentials and unpatched firmware.

questions.stem: Which statement about a rogue AP is NOT true?

options.text: It must copy the name of the company's legitimate wireless network
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: imitating a legitimate SSID describes an evil twin.

options.text: It is an unauthorized access point connected to the wired network
options.rationale: True: this is the definition.

options.text: It can be installed by an employee with no malicious intent
options.rationale: True: convenience installs are common.

options.text: It can act as a backdoor into the internal network
options.rationale: True: it bypasses the controls on the official wireless network.

questions.explanation: A rogue AP is defined by being unauthorized and plugged in inside your network. Imitating a legitimate SSID to lure users is what makes an evil twin.
questions.discriminator_tested: A rogue AP sits inside your network; an evil twin imitates a legitimate SSID.

questions.stem: A security sweep finds two problems. In case 1, an attacker's hotspot in the parking lot broadcasts the company's SSID to lure employees. In case 2, a contractor's access point is plugged into a conference room network jack. Which labels are correct?

options.text: Case 1: evil twin; case 2: rogue AP
options.rationale: Correct: case 1 imitates the SSID to target users, and case 2 is an unauthorized AP inside the network.

options.text: Case 1: rogue AP; case 2: evil twin
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Both are rogue APs
options.rationale: The parking lot hotspot is not connected to the company network; it imitates the SSID instead.

options.text: Case 1: on-path attack; case 2: VLAN hopping
options.rationale: Neither label names the device; nothing here involves VLAN tags.

questions.explanation: An evil twin imitates a legitimate SSID and targets users. A rogue AP is any unauthorized access point connected inside the network, whatever its name.
questions.discriminator_tested: An evil twin targets users with a copied SSID; a rogue AP is inside the network.

questions.stem: Which statement about ransomware is NOT accurate?

options.text: It always steals a copy of the victim's data
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is inaccurate: the data is held hostage, not necessarily stolen.

options.text: It encrypts data and demands payment for the key
options.rationale: Accurate: this is the definition.

options.text: It is a form of extortion
options.rationale: Accurate: payment is demanded to restore access.

options.text: Good offline backups reduce its impact
options.rationale: Accurate: restoring from backup avoids needing the attacker's key.

questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment for the key. It is extortion for access; the data is held, not necessarily stolen.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ransomware holds data for payment; it is not necessarily stolen.

questions.stem: Which control most directly reduces Trojan infections across a company's laptops?

options.text: Allow only approved software from trusted sources to be installed
options.rationale: Correct: a Trojan needs the user to install and run it.

options.text: Change the native VLAN on trunk links
options.rationale: That counters VLAN hopping.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping
options.rationale: That stops rogue DHCP servers.

options.text: Block common passwords
options.rationale: That counters dictionary attacks.

questions.explanation: A Trojan is malicious code disguised as legitimate software. Because it needs the user to run it and does not self-replicate, controlling what users can install is the most direct defense.
questions.discriminator_tested: A Trojan needs the user to run it; it does not spread by itself.

questions.stem: Within minutes, malware appears on hundreds of unpatched servers across the network. No user opened a file or clicked anything; each infected server scans for and infects others over the network. What type of malware is this?

options.text: Worm
options.rationale: Correct: self-replicating over the network with no user action.

options.text: Virus
options.rationale: A virus needs a host file and a user action to spread.

options.text: Trojan
options.rationale: A Trojan must be run by a user and does not self-replicate.

options.text: Rootkit
options.rationale: A rootkit is defined by hiding, not by spreading.

questions.explanation: A worm self-replicates over networks with no user action and no host file, which is why it can spread so quickly through unpatched systems.
questions.discriminator_tested: A worm spreads with no user action and no host file.

questions.stem: Several programs on a PC have grown in size. The malicious code runs only when someone opens one of those programs, and it reaches other machines only when infected programs are copied to them and run there. What is it?

options.text: Virus
options.rationale: Correct: it attaches to host programs and needs a user to run them.

options.text: Worm
options.rationale: A worm spreads by itself across the network without a host file.

options.text: Trojan
options.rationale: A Trojan is a standalone disguised program; it does not infect other files.

options.text: Keylogger
options.rationale: A keylogger records keystrokes; it is not defined by how it spreads.

questions.explanation: A virus attaches to a legitimate file or program and needs a user action to run and spread. That host-plus-user requirement separates it from a worm.
questions.discriminator_tested: A virus needs a host file and a user action.

questions.stem: A free VPN app shows no ads and doesn't slow the phone, but it quietly sends the user's browsing history, contacts, and location to an unknown server. It also records some keystrokes. Which category best describes the app's overall purpose?

options.text: Spyware
options.rationale: Correct: its purpose is covert collection of many kinds of user data.

options.text: Keylogger
options.rationale: Keystroke capture is only one of its methods; the app gathers much more.

options.text: Adware
options.rationale: The app shows no ads.

options.text: Ransomware
options.rationale: Nothing is encrypted and no payment is demanded.

questions.explanation: Spyware secretly collects user activity and data. A keylogger is a narrower capture method that spyware may include, so the keystroke detail is a distractor.
questions.discriminator_tested: Spyware's goal is covert information gathering; keylogging is one possible method.

questions.stem: Which two statements about keyloggers are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: They record keystrokes to capture credentials and other input
options.rationale: Correct: this is the definition.

options.text: They are often delivered by a Trojan or spyware
options.rationale: Correct: a keylogger is a capture method usually carried by other malware.

options.text: HTTPS defeats them because the traffic is encrypted
options.rationale: Keystrokes are captured on the device before any encryption happens.

options.text: They spread across networks on their own
options.rationale: Self-spreading describes a worm.

options.text: Their main purpose is to display unwanted ads
options.rationale: That describes adware.

questions.explanation: A keylogger is a specific capture method that records keystrokes on the endpoint. It is often delivered by spyware or a Trojan, and it captures input before encryption can protect it.
questions.discriminator_tested: A keylogger is a keystroke-capture method, often delivered by other malware.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly separates a rootkit from other malware?

options.text: It hides itself and other malware deep in the OS, kernel, or firmware to keep privileged access
options.rationale: Correct: concealment is what defines a rootkit.

options.text: It encrypts files and demands a ransom
options.rationale: That defines ransomware.

options.text: It self-replicates across networks
options.rationale: That defines a worm.

options.text: It displays unwanted advertisements
options.rationale: That defines adware.

questions.explanation: A rootkit is defined by concealment. It embeds deep in the system to keep stealthy, privileged access and hides itself and other malware from tools running on the infected system.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rootkits are defined by concealment.

questions.stem: Which statement about adware is NOT true?

options.text: It reaches users only through ad networks on legitimate websites, with nothing installed on the device
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: that describes malvertising.

options.text: It is often bundled with free software
options.rationale: True: free installers are a common delivery route.

options.text: It delivers unwanted ads
options.rationale: True: this is its main behavior.

options.text: It can track browsing and slow the device
options.rationale: True: tracking and performance loss are common side effects.

questions.explanation: Adware is software installed on the device, often bundled with free programs, that serves unwanted ads. Malicious ads delivered through ad networks on legitimate sites are malvertising.
questions.discriminator_tested: Adware is installed on the device; malvertising rides on ad networks.

questions.stem: Which two statements correctly separate malvertising from adware? (Choose two.)

options.text: Malvertising is delivered through ad networks on legitimate websites
options.rationale: Correct: the attack rides on the ad network.

options.text: Adware is software installed on the user's device
options.rationale: Correct: it is often bundled with free software.

options.text: Malvertising requires the hosting website's servers to be hacked
options.rationale: The site itself isn't compromised; the bad ad comes from the ad network.

options.text: Adware arrives only through ad networks, without anything being installed
options.rationale: That describes malvertising, not adware.

options.text: Malvertising is only a harmless nuisance
options.rationale: Malvertising can redirect to or deliver malware.

questions.explanation: Malvertising places malicious ads on legitimate sites through ad networks without compromising the site. Adware is software on the victim's device that serves unwanted ads.
questions.discriminator_tested: Malvertising rides on ad networks; adware is installed software.

questions.stem: An authentication log shows one account receiving the guesses 'aaaa', 'aaab', 'aaac', 'aaad', and so on, thousands of times per minute. Which attack is this?

options.text: Brute force attack
options.rationale: Correct: it works through every possible combination in order.

options.text: Dictionary attack
options.rationale: A dictionary attack tries likely words from a list, not every combination.

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: Shoulder surfing is watching someone type, not automated guessing.

options.text: Keylogger
options.rationale: A keylogger captures the real password; nothing is being guessed.

questions.explanation: A brute force attack tries every possible combination. It is exhaustive and slow, and it is defeated by account lockouts and longer passwords.
questions.discriminator_tested: Brute force is exhaustive; dictionary attacks try only likely passwords.

questions.stem: An attacker is running a wordlist of common and previously leaked passwords against employee accounts. Which two controls most directly reduce the chance this dictionary attack succeeds? (Choose two.)

options.text: Reject passwords that appear on common or leaked-password lists
options.rationale: Correct: it removes the exact guesses on the attacker's list.

options.text: Lock accounts after a small number of failed attempts
options.rationale: Correct: the attacker cannot get through enough of the list.

options.text: Require users to change their passwords every 30 days
options.rationale: Frequent changes don't help if users keep picking common passwords.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping
options.rationale: DHCP snooping stops rogue DHCP servers.

options.text: Change the native VLAN
options.rationale: That counters double-tagging VLAN hopping.

questions.explanation: A dictionary attack guesses likely passwords from a precompiled list. Blocking common passwords removes those guesses, and lockouts limit how many can be tried.
questions.discriminator_tested: A dictionary attack guesses likely passwords from a list.

questions.stem: Investigators find that an outside group has had quiet access to a defense contractor's network for 14 months, slowly collecting engineering files while avoiding detection. Which term fits best?

options.text: Advanced persistent threat (APT)
options.rationale: Correct: a stealthy, long-term, targeted intrusion.

options.text: Ransomware
options.rationale: Ransomware is overt and demands payment; this attacker stayed hidden.

options.text: DDoS
options.rationale: A DDoS attacks availability; this attack quietly took data.

options.text: Insider threat
options.rationale: The group is outside the organization and had no legitimate access.

questions.explanation: An APT is a stealthy, long-term, targeted intrusion, often by a well-resourced group. It is defined by persistence and dwell time.
questions.discriminator_tested: APT is defined by persistence and dwell time.

questions.stem: A new batch of IP cameras is taken over within hours of being connected, even though no firmware vulnerability has been published for them. Logs show successful logins using the vendor's documented admin username and password. Which step would most directly have prevented this?

options.text: Changing the default credentials before deployment
options.rationale: Correct: the attackers simply used the published login.

options.text: Upgrading the cameras' firmware
options.rationale: There was no known firmware flaw; the attackers logged in with valid default credentials.

options.text: Enabling DHCP snooping
options.rationale: That stops rogue DHCP servers, not logins.

options.text: Changing the native VLAN
options.rationale: That counters double-tagging VLAN hopping.

questions.explanation: Default credentials are published by vendors and widely abused. Changing default credentials before deployment closes that door; the firmware detail is a distractor.
questions.discriminator_tested: Changing default credentials counters default-login exploitation.

questions.stem: A company's password filter rejects any new password found on a list of millions of common and previously leaked passwords. Which attack does this control mainly address?

options.text: Dictionary attack
options.rationale: Correct: it removes the likely passwords that a wordlist would try.

options.text: Brute force attack
options.rationale: Brute force tries every combination; blocking some common passwords barely shrinks that search.

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: Any password, common or not, can be watched as it is typed.

options.text: Keylogger
options.rationale: A keylogger captures whatever password is typed, however uncommon.

questions.explanation: Avoiding common passwords removes the guesses a dictionary list contains. It does little against attacks that capture the real password or try every combination.
questions.discriminator_tested: Blocking common passwords counters dictionary attacks.

questions.stem: Which statement about DHCP snooping is NOT true?

options.text: It encrypts DHCP messages so attackers cannot read them
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: DHCP snooping filters DHCP messages; it does not encrypt them.

options.text: It is a feature configured on switches
options.rationale: True: the switch enforces it.

options.text: It classifies switch ports as trusted or untrusted
options.rationale: True: only trusted ports may send DHCP offers.

options.text: It drops DHCP offers arriving on untrusted ports
options.rationale: True: this is how it blocks rogue servers.

questions.explanation: DHCP snooping is a switch feature that accepts DHCP offers only from trusted ports, which counters rogue DHCP servers. It filters traffic; it does not encrypt it.
questions.discriminator_tested: DHCP snooping uses trusted and untrusted ports to counter rogue DHCP.

questions.stem: An attacker on an access port reached a server VLAN by sending double-tagged frames. The trunk links still use the default native VLAN 1, which is also the attacker's access VLAN. What made this possible?

options.text: The attacker's access VLAN matched the trunk's native VLAN, which was left at the default
options.rationale: Correct: double tagging relies on the native VLAN's tag being stripped.

options.text: DHCP snooping was disabled
options.rationale: DHCP snooping protects against rogue DHCP servers, not VLAN tagging.

options.text: The servers' firmware was out of date
options.rationale: The attack abused switch VLAN configuration, not server code.

options.text: Users chose common passwords
options.rationale: No passwords were involved in reaching the VLAN.

questions.explanation: Double tagging exploits the native VLAN on trunk links. Changing the native VLAN from the default to an unused ID removes the root cause.
questions.discriminator_tested: Changing the native VLAN counters double-tagging VLAN hopping.

questions.stem: A worm is spreading by exploiting a known flaw in a web server application. The vendor released a fix for this flaw last month. Which action most directly closes the hole?

options.text: Apply the vendor's software update to the web server application
options.rationale: Correct: patching removes the vulnerability the worm exploits.

options.text: Upgrade the server hardware's firmware
options.rationale: The flaw is in application software, not in embedded device code.

options.text: Change the default credentials on the server
options.rationale: The worm exploits a software flaw; it does not log in.

options.text: Change the native VLAN
options.rationale: That counters VLAN hopping.

questions.explanation: Patching and updating fix known vulnerabilities in operating systems and applications. Firmware upgrades are for code embedded in hardware.
questions.discriminator_tested: Patching fixes software (OS and app) flaws; firmware is device-level code.

questions.stem: Which statement about upgrading firmware is NOT accurate?

options.text: It is the same task as installing operating system patches
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is inaccurate: firmware is device-level code, separate from OS and application patching.

options.text: It updates code embedded in hardware
options.rationale: Accurate: this is what firmware is.

options.text: It can fix vulnerabilities in routers, switches, and IoT devices
options.rationale: Accurate: these devices run firmware.

options.text: A corrupted firmware image can leave a device unusable
options.rationale: Accurate: this is exactly what a permanent DoS exploits.

questions.explanation: Upgrading firmware updates the code embedded in hardware. It is a separate task from patching operating systems and applications.
questions.discriminator_tested: Firmware is embedded device code; contrast with OS and app patching.

questions.stem: A phishing email gets past the spam filter, and an employee clicks its link. Endpoint protection then blocks the malware download, and network monitoring raises an alert about the attempt. Which security principle does this outcome illustrate?

options.text: Defense in depth
options.rationale: Correct: when one layer failed, the next layers still stopped the attack.

options.text: Social engineering
options.rationale: Social engineering is the attack technique, not the defensive principle.

options.text: Patching and updating
options.rationale: Patching is a single control; the outcome came from several layers.

options.text: Change default credentials
options.rationale: No default logins were involved.

questions.explanation: Defense in depth layers overlapping controls so that no single control is relied on. Here the email filter failed, but endpoint protection and monitoring still caught the attack.
questions.discriminator_tested: Defense in depth: no single control is relied on.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a social engineering technique?

options.text: A SYN flood against a web server
options.rationale: Correct choice: it is a technical attack on a system, with no one being manipulated.

options.text: Tailgating through a secure door
options.rationale: Social engineering: it exploits people's behavior at an entrance.

options.text: A vishing call from someone pretending to be IT
options.rationale: Social engineering: it deceives a person by phone.

options.text: A spear phishing email to a payroll clerk
options.rationale: Social engineering: it manipulates a specific person.

questions.explanation: Social engineering manipulates people rather than systems. Phishing variants and physical-access tricks fit; a SYN flood attacks a system directly.
questions.discriminator_tested: Social engineering targets people, not systems.

questions.stem: What most clearly separates an insider threat from an external attack?

options.text: The person already has legitimate access, whether they act maliciously or by accident
options.rationale: Correct: legitimate access is the defining feature.

options.text: The person must intend to cause harm
options.rationale: Accidental harm by someone with access also counts as an insider threat.

options.text: The person must use malware
options.rationale: Insiders often misuse access they already have, with no malware.

options.text: The attack must happen outside business hours
options.rationale: Timing has nothing to do with the definition.

questions.explanation: Insider threats come from people who already have legitimate access, inside the perimeter. Their intent can be malicious or accidental.
questions.discriminator_tested: Insiders already have legitimate access; intent can be malicious or accidental.

questions.stem: Which statement about plain phishing, as opposed to its targeted forms, is NOT accurate?

options.text: It is tailored to one specific person using personal details
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is inaccurate: tailoring makes it spear phishing.

options.text: It typically arrives as email
options.rationale: Accurate: email is the usual medium.

options.text: It is broad and untargeted
options.rationale: Accurate: the same message goes to many people.

options.text: It aims to steal credentials or data
options.rationale: Accurate: that is its usual goal.

questions.explanation: Phishing is a broad, untargeted fraudulent message, typically email. Tailoring it with personal details makes it spear phishing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Phishing is broad and untargeted; spear phishing is tailored.

questions.stem: An employee gets a text message: 'Call IT now about your locked account.' When the employee calls the number, a person posing as IT asks for the password, and the employee says it aloud. Which term describes the step in which the password was actually obtained?

options.text: Vishing
options.rationale: Correct: the password was handed over during a voice call.

options.text: Smishing
options.rationale: The text message started the attack, but the password was obtained by voice.

options.text: Spear phishing
options.rationale: Nothing shows the message was tailored with personal details.

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: No one watched the employee type anything.

questions.explanation: Vishing is phishing by voice or phone. The medium of the step decides the label, so the opening text message is a distractor for this question.
questions.discriminator_tested: Vishing medium = voice; smishing medium = text.

questions.stem: Which two are examples of smishing? (Choose two.)

options.text: An SMS claiming a parcel fee is due, with a payment link
options.rationale: Correct: phishing delivered by text message.

options.text: A text message from 'your bank' asking you to reply with your PIN
options.rationale: Correct: also delivered by SMS.

options.text: A phone call from a fake fraud department
options.rationale: A voice call is vishing.

options.text: An email sent unchanged to millions of addresses
options.rationale: That is ordinary email phishing.

options.text: A fake Wi-Fi network named after a café
options.rationale: That is an evil twin.

questions.explanation: Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS or text message; the medium is what defines it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Smishing medium = text message.

questions.stem: Which two details show that an email is spear phishing rather than ordinary phishing? (Choose two.)

options.text: It addresses the recipient by name and mentions their real manager
options.rationale: Correct: personal details show it was tailored.

options.text: It refers to a project the recipient's team is actually working on
options.rationale: Correct: inside knowledge shows targeting.

options.text: It was sent unchanged to thousands of random addresses
options.rationale: Mass, untargeted sending is ordinary phishing.

options.text: It arrived as a text message
options.rationale: Text delivery makes it smishing, which says nothing about targeting.

options.text: It asks the reader to click a link
options.rationale: Almost all phishing does this, targeted or not.

questions.explanation: Spear phishing is tailored to a specific person or group using personal detail. Broad, identical messages are ordinary phishing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Spear phishing is targeted and uses personal detail.

questions.stem: Which statement about whaling is NOT true?

options.text: It means any phishing message that uses urgent language
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: urgency is common in all phishing; whaling is about who is targeted.

options.text: It targets executives or other high-value people
options.rationale: True: target seniority defines it.

options.text: It is a form of spear phishing
options.rationale: True: it is targeted phishing aimed high.

options.text: It often impersonates trusted parties such as lawyers or board members
options.rationale: True: impersonating people executives trust is common.

questions.explanation: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at executives or other high-value targets. The seniority of the target, not the tone of the message, is the differentiator.
questions.discriminator_tested: Whaling = spear phishing aimed at executives.

questions.stem: Which control most directly prevents tailgating at a badge-controlled entrance?

options.text: A mantrap or turnstile that admits only one person per badge swipe
options.rationale: Correct: no one can follow an authorized person through.

options.text: Phishing awareness training
options.rationale: That targets email-based attacks, not physical entry.

options.text: Privacy screens on monitors
options.rationale: Privacy screens counter shoulder surfing.

options.text: Account lockout after failed logins
options.rationale: Lockouts stop password guessing, not physical entry.

questions.explanation: Tailgating means following an authorized person through a secured entry without their knowledge. A control that admits exactly one person per badge removes the opportunity.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tailgating exploits an unknowing authorized person at a shared entry.

questions.stem: Security video shows an employee badging in, then waving a visitor without a badge through the door and saying 'go ahead.' The employee later says they assumed the visitor was allowed. What happened?

options.text: Piggybacking
options.rationale: Correct: the employee knowingly let the visitor in.

options.text: Tailgating
options.rationale: Tailgating happens without the employee's knowledge; this employee waved the visitor through.

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: Shoulder surfing is watching screens or keypads.

options.text: Vishing
options.rationale: Vishing happens over the phone.

questions.explanation: Piggybacking is entry with an authorized person's knowledge or consent. The employee's good intentions don't change that, and it is what separates piggybacking from tailgating.
questions.discriminator_tested: Piggybacking: the authorized person knowingly lets them in.

questions.stem: Days after an employee unlocked their phone on a crowded train, someone else unlocks it on the first try. The phone has no malware, and the PIN was never sent anywhere. How was the PIN most likely captured?

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: Correct: someone watched the PIN being entered.

options.text: A keylogger
options.rationale: A keylogger is software, and the phone has no malware.

options.text: An on-path attack
options.rationale: The PIN never crossed a network, so there was nothing to intercept.

options.text: A brute force attack
options.rationale: Guessing on the device would show failed attempts; the PIN worked first time.

questions.explanation: Shoulder surfing captures information by watching screens or keypads, with no technical exploit, which fits a crowded train and a clean phone.
questions.discriminator_tested: Shoulder surfing is visual observation with no technical exploit.
